confidence_rationale: The closest existing analogue to ARC-019's own falsifier design, and the reason this entry carries the highest confidence in the directory. Wu et al. run thousands of orderings under a matched budget with a random-ordering control that isolates the confound ARC-019's non-degeneracy precondition is groping toward: any apparent curriculum benefit on standard benchmarks is attributable to the *dynamic training-set size*, not to the ordering, because random-curriculum matches or beats curriculum. That is a direct weakening. But the same paper finds curricula do help under a limited training-time budget or with noisy data -- and REE's regime is exactly limited-budget and noisy -- so the honest direction is mixed, not weakens. Held below 0.8 by domain distance: supervised image classification with example-level difficulty ordering, not embodied phase-advance gating.
failure_signatures: Any REE staged-vs-flat advantage may be an artefact of the staged arm's smaller effective early training set rather than of the gate ordering; without a random-ordering (or shuffled-phase) control at matched budget, a positive V3 result cannot distinguish these and would not license ARC-019.

Wu et al. report curricula are beneficial only under limited budget or label noise, so a staged-arm advantage observed at a small episode budget may vanish at a larger one -- a REE experiment that measures one budget cannot claim staging is architecturally load-bearing, only that it is budget-efficient at that point.

mapping.source_claim_statement: For standard benchmark datasets, curricula have only marginal benefits, and randomly ordered samples perform as well or better than curricula and anti-curricula, suggesting that any benefit is entirely due to the dynamic training set size; curriculum (but not anti-curriculum) can improve performance either with limited training time budget or in existence of noisy data.
mapping.ree_translation: For ARC-019 this splits the claim in two. The strong reading -- explicit stage/gate structure improves outcome quality at matched total budget -- is the one Wu et al. find no support for in their setting, and their random-curriculum control is the design REE's staged-vs-flat comparison currently lacks. The weak reading -- staging is a budget- and noise-efficiency device -- survives, and is the reading REE's own regime (sparse, noisy, episode-budget-constrained developmental training) most plausibly falls under.
mapping.mapping_caveat: The curriculum here is an ordering over *training examples by difficulty* in i.i.d. supervised learning. REE's is an ordering over *environment/task phases with competence gates* in a sequential embodied setting where later phases are not merely harder but structurally unavailable until earlier competences exist. That structural dependency has no analogue in CIFAR, so a null result there does not straightforwardly transfer; what does transfer is the methodological demand for a set-size control.
mapping.source_context: CIFAR10 / CIFAR100 / CIFAR100 with noisy labels; thousands of example orderings; supervised image classification; ICLR 2021 oral.

confidence_components.notes: Highest source quality in this pull: large-scale systematic ablation, ICLR oral, public code. Transfer risk is nonetheless high because the i.i.d. supervised setting removes the structural phase-dependency that is REE's actual reason for gating. Aggregate is pulled above the component mean because the paper's *methodological* contribution (the random-ordering control) transfers even where its empirical result does not.
